# **Mildenhall et al. (2020):** NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis

## One fit <em>is</em> one scene: **31.01 PSNR** against 26.05 for the best baseline (NV) on realistic synthetic scenes, in 5 MB of weights where LLFF stores more than 15 GB

<p class="byline">UC Berkeley, Google Research, UC San Diego · ECCV 2020, arXiv March 2020</p>

<p class="links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08934">arXiv</a><a class="project" href="https://www.matthewtancik.com/nerf">project page</a><a href="https://github.com/bmild/nerf">code</a><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuH79E8rdKc">video</a></p>

<p class="byline"><em>Dashed underlines are fact-checked against the paper — hover one to read the note.</em></p>

---

<a class="slide-id" id="2b8e5d31-77c4-42fa-8e63-9d1a0f4c1122"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## TL;DR

- **What it is** — **one small MLP that stores one scene**, so you can render that scene from **new cameras nobody photographed**, from **tens of posed photos and nothing else** — posed meaning each photo's camera position, orientation and intrinsics are known, with near and far scene bounds ([slide 21](#21)).
- **The trick** — the scene is **a continuous (x, y, z, θ, φ) → (RGB, σ) function** of a 3D point and a viewing direction, where σ is volume density, how strongly that point stops a ray; and an image is **a volume-rendering integral along each ray** — which is **differentiable**, so squared pixel error trains it.
- **The stabilisers** — **positional encoding** lifts coordinates into <span class="term" data-tiphead="Why a fixed lift helps" data-tip="Rahaman et al. showed deep networks are biased toward low-frequency functions. Replacing each coordinate by sines and cosines at doubling frequencies makes nearby points easy to tell apart, so the MLP can fit sharp edges instead of a blur. It has no parameters and learns nothing.">doubling-frequency sines</span> (10 frequencies for position, 4 for direction), and a **coarse-to-fine sampler** aims 128 extra samples where the ray stops.
- **The numbers** — on the realistic synthetic scenes, **31.01** <span class="term" data-tiphead="PSNR" data-tip="Peak signal-to-noise ratio: the mean squared pixel error on a log scale, in decibels. Higher is better; plus 3 dB means roughly half the squared error, and differences of a few tenths are usually invisible.">PSNR</span> against **26.05 for the best baseline**, <span class="term" data-tiphead="NV, Neural Volumes" data-tip="Lombardi et al. 2019. A 3D convolutional network, optimised per scene, predicts a 128-cubed RGB-alpha voxel grid plus a warp grid, and novel views are rendered by marching rays through it. Objects must sit in a bounded volume in front of a separately captured background.">NV</span> *(Table 1)*; **5 MB** of weights against **over 15 GB** of grids for <span class="term" data-tiphead="LLFF, Local Light Field Fusion" data-tip="Mildenhall et al. 2019. One 3D convolutional network, trained once on a large dataset, turns each input photo of a new scene into a multiplane image; novel views blend nearby MPIs. No per-scene training, which is why it takes minutes and stores gigabytes.">LLFF</span>: **3000×** smaller *(Sec. 6.3)*.
- **Why it mattered** — coordinate networks displaced voxel grids; ancestor of [mip-NeRF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.13415), [Instant-NGP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.05989) and, by reaction, [3D Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04079).

<a class="slide-id" id="1b2c3d4e-5f6a-4b7c-8d9e-0f1a2b3c4d5e"></a>

## The core idea — store a function, not a scene

- **Why care:** the scene used to be **a discretised grid** — LLFF needs **over 15 GB** per scene; NV's **128³ voxels** cap detail outright.
- **What prior work does:** train a **CNN that outputs that grid** — resolution bought with memory, cubically.
- **What this paper does instead:** keep the scene **continuous**, as **one MLP, no convolutions**; never materialise a grid.
- **The enabling fact:** volume rendering is **naturally differentiable**, so *"the only input required to optimize our representation is a set of images with known camera poses"*.
- **Lifted from:** the integral is Kajiya and Von Herzen's [volume rendering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volume_rendering) (1984); the low-frequency bias behind the encoding is [Rahaman et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.08734)

---

<a class="slide-id" id="2c3d4e5f-6a7b-4c8d-9e0f-1a2b3c4d5e6f"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## The five Cs, in one look

Five Cs — a standard first-pass checklist for a paper: Category, Context, Correctness, Contributions, Clarity.

- **Category** — an **empirical method paper**: a scene representation, plus the renderer that makes it trainable.
- **Context** — against voxel and <span class="term" data-tiphead="MPI, multiplane image" data-tip="A stack of semi-transparent RGB-alpha planes at fixed depths in front of one camera. A new view is rendered by alpha compositing the planes, which works well only for viewpoints near that camera.">MPI</span> grids ([NV](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.07751), [LLFF](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.00889)) and against per-ray coordinate nets (<span class="term" data-tiphead="SRN, Scene Representation Networks" data-tip="Sitzmann et al. 2019. An MLP maps each 3D point to a feature vector, and a learned recurrent ray marcher steps along each ray to find one opaque surface, whose feature is decoded into a single colour. One depth and one colour per ray, so thin or translucent structure is lost.">[SRN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01618)</span>).
- **Correctness** — rests on two things that hold: rendering is **differentiable**, and an MLP fed <span class="term" data-tiphead="Fourier features" data-tip="Each coordinate is replaced by a ladder of sines and cosines at frequencies that double. The MLP's low-frequency bias is then a bias in the lifted space, not in scene space, so sharp edges become learnable.">Fourier features</span> fits high frequencies. Everything else is **reported without seeds or error bars**.
- **Contributions** — the **5D radiance field**; the **differentiable renderer** trained from RGB alone; **positional encoding** and **hierarchical sampling**.
- **Clarity** — very high: Figure 2 carries the method, Figure 4 the ablation, Section 4 the derivation.

---

<a class="slide-id" id="3d4e5f6a-7b8c-4d9e-a0f1-2b3c4d5e6f7a"></a>

## Should you read further?

- **Read §3–5 — the representation, the renderer, and the two training tricks — if** you build or evaluate **3D reconstruction from cameras**: this is the reference frame for neural rendering since. The mechanism is walked through on **[slides 7–21](#7)**, §4 included.
- **Skim §4, the volume-rendering integral and its quadrature, plus Figure 2, if** you only want **the differentiable renderer**. Section 4 spans two pages and it is the transferable idea; it is on **[slides 11–16](#11)**.
- **Read §6, results and ablations, if** you need to judge **how far the gains hold** — Tables 1–2 and Figures 5–6 are on **[slides 22–26](#22)**, cost, limits and open challenges on [slides 27–29](#27).
- **Skip it if** you need **speed, dynamic scenes or generalisation** — none of them are here (**[slides 27–28](#27)**). Go to [Instant-NGP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.05989), [D-NeRF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13961) and [pixelNeRF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.02190) respectively.

</div>

- **A NeRF is a lookup you can differentiate**, not a model of scenes: the weights are **that scene's file format**, and a scene is one static capture — one set of posed photos of one object or room, fitted from random weights *(Sec. 3, 5.3)*.

---

<a class="slide-id" id="5eb18064-aaf7-4c2d-b196-c04d3b7f4455"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## The direction reaches colour, but never reaches geometry

- **The conclusion, first:** σ is a function of **position only**, so **every camera sees the same shape**, which the paper says *encourages* multiview consistency rather than guarantees it — and colour is a function of **position and direction**, so cameras are *allowed* to disagree about the **look** *(Sec. 3)*.

<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Why density must ignore direction" data-tip="If density could change with the viewing direction, every training camera could carve out its own private geometry that explains its own pixels and nothing else. <text x="42" y="556" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="17" font-weight="700">consistency mechanism.</text>
</a>

## The paper's own picture of it — two points, two cameras, and the hemisphere of colours each point emits

<figure class="credit"><span style="position:relative; display:inline-block"><img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," width="1040"/><span class="hotspot" data-tiphead="(a) View 1" data-tip="Two fixed 3D points on the Ship scene seen from the first camera: one on the hull (orange inset) and one on the water surface (blue inset)." style="left:0%; width:33%"></span><span class="hotspot" data-tiphead="(b) View 2" data-tip="The same two points from a second camera. The specular appearance of both points changes with where you stand." style="left:33%; width:28%"></span><span class="hotspot" data-tiphead="(c) Radiance distributions" data-tip="For each point, the colour the network emits over the whole hemisphere of viewing directions. Smooth and continuous over the whole hemisphere, and learned only from the training photographs." style="left:61%; width:39%"></span></span><figcaption>Figure 3 from <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08934">Mildenhall et al. 2020</a>, p. 6 — the Ship scene; orange inset: a point on the hull, blue inset: a point on the water.</figcaption></figure>

- **Same two 3D points, two cameras** (a, b): the geometry is shared, and the **colour of both points changes** with the camera.
- **(c) is what the colour head learns** — a whole hemisphere of directions per point; the next slide shows it moving on a real capture.

---

<a class="slide-id" id="6fc29175-bb08-4d3e-c2a7-d1450c804566"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## Same point, same geometry, different colour — on real capture

<figure class="credit"><video class="clip" src="https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~viscomp/projects/LF/papers/ECCV20/nerf/website_renders/viewdirs_website_bww.mp4" style="width:860px;height:329px" data-autoplay muted loop playsinline controls preload="metadata"><a href="https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~viscomp/projects/LF/papers/ECCV20/nerf/website_renders/viewdirs_website_bww.mp4" target="_blank" rel="noopener">viewdirs_website_bww.mp4 on the NeRF project site</a></video><figcaption>Clip from the <a class="project" href="https://www.matthewtancik.com/nerf">project page</a>, section View-Dependent Appearance — not in the PDF.</figcaption></figure>

| what moves | what does not |
|---|---|
| the d **handed to the colour head**, swept by the renderer while the camera stays **fixed** | each pixel's ray, the points it samples, and the density, because **σ never sees d** |

- **How the clip is made:** d is just an input, so the renderer can query a fixed camera's points with **someone else's viewing direction** — geometry stays put, the highlights slide.

---

<a class="slide-id" id="96923788-54a8-49eb-82e2-28b6b957bd8c"></a>

## Figure 2 as printed — four panels (a)–(d); the next slide runs them as five numbered steps

<figure class="credit"><span style="position:relative; display:inline-block"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="1060"/><span class="hotspot" data-tiphead="(a) 5D input" data-tip="Camera rays are marched through the scene and sampled at discrete points; each sample is a position plus the viewing direction of its ray." style="left:0%; width:27%"></span><span class="hotspot" data-tiphead="(b) Output" data-tip="The MLP maps every sample to an emitted colour and a volume density; the density profile along two rays is sketched in red." style="left:27%; width:31%"></span><span class="hotspot" data-tiphead="(c) Volume rendering" data-tip="The colours along one ray are composited into a single pixel, weighted by density and by how much light still reaches the camera at that depth." style="left:58%; width:22%"></span><span class="hotspot" data-tiphead="(d) Rendering loss" data-tip="The rendered pixel is compared with the ground-truth photograph by squared error. The whole chain is differentiable, so this is the only supervision." style="left:80%; width:20%"></span></span><figcaption>Figure 2 from <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08934">Mildenhall et al. 2020</a>, p. 5.</figcaption></figure>

- **(a)** sample 5D coordinates along camera rays → **(b)** the MLP returns colour and density → **(c)** volume rendering composites them into a pixel → **(d)** squared error against the photograph, **differentiable all the way back**.

<text x="802" y="278" class="pipe-d" font-size="14">colour may vary with d</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4.E3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="4 &#183; Composite the samples into one colour" data-tip="The samples along the ray are folded into a single RGB value by the quadrature form of the volume rendering integral. It is ordinary alpha compositing: each sample contributes its colour scaled by how opaque it is and by how much light was still travelling when the ray arrived.">
<rect x="18" y="316" width="551" height="150" rx="12" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#bc8cff" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="42" y="344" fill="#bc8cff" font-weight="700" font-size="15">4 &#183; VOLUME RENDER &#8212; ONE PIXEL COMES OUT</text>
<text x="545" y="344" text-anchor="end" class="pipe-d" font-size="13">Fig. 2 (c)</text>
<text x="42" y="382" class="pipe-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="19">&#264;(r) = &#931; T&#7522; &#945;&#7522; c&#7522;</text>
<text x="42" y="416" class="pipe-m" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="15">&#945;&#7522; = 1 - e^(-&#963;&#7522;&#948;&#7522;) is how opaque one slab is</text>
<text x="42" y="440" class="pipe-m" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="15">T&#7522; = &#928; (1 - &#945;&#11002;) is how much light still arrives</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S5.E6" target="_blank" data-tiphead="5 &#183; Compare with the photograph" data-tip="The rendered colour is compared with the colour that pixel actually has in its training photograph. Squared error, summed over a batch of 4096 rays drawn from all training photographs, for the coarse and the fine render alike. That is the entire training signal.">
<rect x="589" y="316" width="551" height="150" rx="12" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="613" y="344" fill="#f85149" font-weight="700" font-size="15">5 &#183; PHOTOMETRIC LOSS &#8212; THE ONLY SUPERVISION</text>
<text x="1116" y="344" text-anchor="end" class="pipe-d" font-size="13">Fig. 2 (d)</text>
<g data-tiphead="The rendered colour" data-tip="What the current weights predict this pixel should look like from this camera.">
<rect x="613" y="358" width="150" height="52" rx="7" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#93c5fd" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="688" y="379" text-anchor="middle" class="pipe-t" font-size="15">&#264;(r)</text>
<text x="688" y="398" text-anchor="middle" class="pipe-d" font-size="14">rendered</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="The observed colour" data-tip="The colour that pixel already has in the training photograph. No annotation, no preprocessing, no 3D anything.">
<rect x="777" y="358" width="150" height="52" rx="7" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="852" y="379" text-anchor="middle" class="pipe-t" font-size="15">C(r)</text>
<text x="852" y="398" text-anchor="middle" class="pipe-d" font-size="14">the photo</text>
</g>
<text x="951" y="382" class="pipe-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="16">&#8214;&#264;-C&#8214;&#178;</text>
<text x="613" y="432" class="pipe-d" font-size="14">4096 rays per step, from all photos; coarse render scored too</text>
<text x="613" y="454" class="pipe-d" font-size="14">Eq. 6, and nothing else enters the objective</text>
</a>
<path d="M864,470 L864,496 L10,496 L10,168 L14,168" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="2.6" stroke-dasharray="9 6" marker-end="url(#pr)" fill="none"/>
<g data-tiphead="The backward pass" data-tip="The forward pass runs steps 1 to 5; the error then travels this dashed path in reverse. Photometric error differentiates through the compositing sum, through the MLP outputs and into every weight. This dashed path is the only reason the density field ever becomes correct geometry.">
<rect x="150" y="472" width="600" height="28" rx="6" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="450" y="492" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f85149" font-weight="700" font-size="16">&#8706;L / &#8706;&#920; flows back through the quadrature into the weights</text>
</g>
<rect class="pipe-a-s0" x="18" y="44" width="362" height="244" rx="12" fill="rgba(255,255,255,0.03)" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="3" opacity="0.25" pointer-events="none"/>
<rect class="pipe-a-s1" x="398" y="44" width="362" height="244" rx="12" fill="rgba(255,255,255,0.03)" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="3" opacity="0.25" pointer-events="none"/>
<rect class="pipe-a-s2" x="778" y="44" width="362" height="244" rx="12" fill="rgba(255,255,255,0.03)" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="3" opacity="0.25" pointer-events="none"/>
<rect class="pipe-a-s3" x="18" y="316" width="551" height="150" rx="12" fill="rgba(255,255,255,0.03)" stroke="#bc8cff" stroke-width="3" opacity="0.25" pointer-events="none"/>
<rect class="pipe-a-s4" x="589" y="316" width="551" height="150" rx="12" fill="rgba(255,255,255,0.03)" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="3" opacity="0.25" pointer-events="none"/>
<circle class="pipe-a-back" cx="864" cy="470" r="7" fill="#f85149" opacity="0" pointer-events="none"/>
<rect x="18" y="510" width="1122" height="74" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="42" y="540" class="pipe-t" font-size="17">Nothing in this diagram ever sees 3D ground truth</text>
<text x="42" y="568" class="pipe-d" font-size="15">No meshes, no depth maps, no voxel targets, no point clouds. The inputs are posed photographs; the loss is measured in pixels.</text>
</svg>
</div>

<a class="slide-id" id="81e4b397-dd2a-4f40-e4c9-f3672ea26788"></a>

## Equation 1 is three factors, and one of them is not obvious

<p style="text-align:center; margin:0 0 2px"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="700" style="background:#fff; border-radius:6px; padding:3px 10px"/></p>
<p class="ev" style="text-align:center; margin:0">Equation 1 as printed in <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08934">Mildenhall et al. 2020</a>, p. 5 — the figure takes it apart.</p>
<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.2rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="860" height="445" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">
<style>.inte-t{fill:#f0f0f0;font-weight:700}.inte-m{font-family:'JetBrains Mono',monospace}.inte-d{fill:#a0a0a0}.inte-hd{fill:#3b82f6;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.05em}</style>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="18" y="28" class="inte-hd" font-size="16">EQUATION 1 &#8212; the expected colour of one camera ray</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4.E1" target="_blank"><text x="1142" y="28" text-anchor="end" class="inte-d" font-size="14">Sec. 4, Eq. 1</text></a>
<text x="42" y="102" class="inte-t" font-size="30">C(r)</text>
<text x="106" y="102" class="inte-d" font-size="30">=</text>
<text x="148" y="110" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="46" font-weight="700">&#8747;</text>
<text x="150" y="130" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15" font-weight="700">near</text>
<text x="150" y="68" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15" font-weight="700">far</text>
<text x="196" y="102" fill="#3fb950" font-size="30" font-weight="700">T(t)</text>
<text x="278" y="102" fill="#f0883e" font-size="30" font-weight="700">&#963;(r(t))</text>
<text x="410" y="102" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="30" font-weight="700">c(r(t), d)</text>
<text x="576" y="102" class="inte-d" font-size="30">dt</text>
<path d="M192,118 L268,118 M192,118 L192,126 M268,118 L268,126" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/>
<path d="M274,118 L402,118 M274,118 L274,126 M402,118 L402,126" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/>
<path d="M406,118 L566,118 M406,118 L406,126 M566,118 L566,126" stroke="#bc8cff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/>
<text x="230" y="146" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3fb950" font-size="15" font-weight="700">how much light</text>
<text x="230" y="165" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3fb950" font-size="15" font-weight="700">still gets here</text>
<text x="338" y="146" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0883e" font-size="15" font-weight="700">how much of it</text>
<text x="338" y="165" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0883e" font-size="15" font-weight="700">stops here</text>
<text x="486" y="146" text-anchor="middle" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="15" font-weight="700">what colour</text>
<text x="486" y="165" text-anchor="middle" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="15" font-weight="700">this point emits</text>
<rect x="622" y="52" width="518" height="132" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="644" y="82" class="inte-t" font-size="17">Read it as an expectation</text>
<text x="644" y="110" class="inte-d" font-size="15">Walk the ray. At every point ask: is light still</text>
<text x="644" y="132" class="inte-d" font-size="15">travelling, does it stop here, what colour is here?</text>
<text x="644" y="162" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15" font-weight="700">The pixel is the average colour where it stops.</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="T(t), accumulated transmittance" data-tip="The probability that the ray travels from the near bound to t without hitting any other particle. It starts at exactly 1 at the near bound and can only fall, because the integral in its exponent only grows. This is the occlusion term: it is why a wall hides what is behind it, and it is the only part of Equation 1 that looks backwards along the ray.">
<rect x="18" y="200" width="1122" height="136" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="42" y="230" fill="#3fb950" font-size="19" font-weight="700">T(t)</text>
<text x="112" y="230" class="inte-t" font-size="17">accumulated transmittance &#8212; the term you cannot guess</text>
<text x="42" y="264" class="inte-m" fill="#3fb950" font-size="17">T(t) = exp( - &#8747; from near to t of &#963;(r(s)) ds )</text>
<text x="42" y="294" class="inte-d" font-size="15">The probability the ray survives from the near bound to t un-occluded.</text>
<text x="42" y="316" class="inte-d" font-size="15">Starts at 1, only ever falls, and mutes everything behind the first opaque thing.</text>
<g data-tiphead="The shape of T along a ray" data-tip="Flat and near 1 through empty space, then a cliff at the first opaque surface, then flat and near zero for the rest of the ray.">
<rect x="928" y="216" width="196" height="104" rx="8" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<path d="M948,306 L1108,306" stroke="#3a3a3a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<path d="M948,232 L948,306" stroke="#3a3a3a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<path d="M948,238 L1014,244 L1042,298 L1108,302" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2.4" fill="none"/>
<text x="958" y="262" class="inte-d" font-size="14">T = 1</text>
<text x="1102" y="288" text-anchor="end" class="inte-d" font-size="14">T = 0</text>
</g>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Sigma, volume density" data-tip="The differential probability of a ray terminating at an infinitesimal particle at that location. Not a colour and not an opacity by itself: it is a rate, so what a slab of thickness delta actually blocks is 1 minus exp of minus sigma times delta. It is a function of position alone.">
<rect x="18" y="352" width="551" height="110" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="42" y="380" fill="#f0883e" font-size="19" font-weight="700">&#963;(r(t))</text>
<text x="132" y="380" class="inte-t" font-size="17">volume density here</text>
<text x="42" y="408" class="inte-d" font-size="15">The differential probability of a ray terminating at an</text>
<text x="42" y="428" class="inte-d" font-size="15">infinitesimal particle there &#8212; a rate, not an opacity, and it</text>
<text x="42" y="448" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15" font-weight="700">depends on position only, never on direction.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="c, emitted colour" data-tip="The RGB the point sends back along direction d. Because it takes the direction as an input, the same point can look white to one camera and orange to another, which is how the model reproduces highlights and reflections. There is no light source in the model: the colour is emitted, so the lighting is baked in.">
<rect x="589" y="352" width="551" height="110" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#bc8cff" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="613" y="380" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="19" font-weight="700">c(r(t), d)</text>
<text x="736" y="380" class="inte-t" font-size="17">colour toward the camera</text>
<text x="613" y="408" class="inte-d" font-size="15">Takes the viewing direction, so one point can look white</text>
<text x="613" y="428" class="inte-d" font-size="15">from here and orange from there. No light source exists:</text>
<text x="613" y="448" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15" font-weight="700">the lighting is baked into the emitted radiance.</text>
</a>
<rect x="18" y="478" width="1122" height="104" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="42" y="508" class="inte-t" font-size="17">What is actually being accumulated</text>
<text x="42" y="536" class="inte-d" font-size="15">T(t)&#183;&#963;(t) is a density over where along the ray the light stops. It integrates to at most 1: the rest is transmitted past the far bound.</text>
<text x="42" y="560" class="inte-d" font-size="15">Integrate colour against that density and you get the pixel. Slide 17 works it through, including what fills the remainder.</text>
</svg>
</div>

<a class="slide-id" id="92f5c4a8-ee3b-4051-f5da-04783bb37899"></a>

## Transmittance is why a wall hides what is behind it

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.4rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="980" height="507" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">
<style>.tran-t{fill:#f0f0f0;font-weight:700}.tran-m{font-family:'JetBrains Mono',monospace}.tran-d{fill:#a0a0a0}.tran-hd{fill:#3b82f6;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.05em}@keyframes tran-a-ball{0.0%{transform:translateX(0);opacity:1}70.0%{transform:translateX(1004px);opacity:1}73.0%{opacity:0}100.0%{transform:translateX(1004px);opacity:0}}.tran-a-ball{animation:tran-a-ball 9s linear infinite}.tran-a-T{stroke-dasharray:419}@keyframes tran-a-T{0.0%{stroke-dashoffset:419}70.0%{stroke-dashoffset:0}100.0%{stroke-dashoffset:0}}.tran-a-T{animation:tran-a-T 9s linear infinite}@keyframes tran-a-b0{0.0%{opacity:0.25}6.2%{opacity:0.25}9.2%{opacity:1}100.0%{opacity:1}}.tran-a-b0{animation:tran-a-b0 9s linear infinite}@keyframes tran-a-b1{0.0%{opacity:0.25}16.0%{opacity:0.25}19.0%{opacity:1}100.0%{opacity:1}}.tran-a-b1{animation:tran-a-b1 9s linear infinite}@keyframes tran-a-b2{0.0%{opacity:0.25}25.6%{opacity:0.25}28.6%{opacity:1}100.0%{opacity:1}}.tran-a-b2{animation:tran-a-b2 9s linear infinite}@keyframes tran-a-b3{0.0%{opacity:0.25}40.6%{opacity:0.25}43.6%{opacity:1}100.0%{opacity:1}}.tran-a-b3{animation:tran-a-b3 9s linear infinite}@keyframes tran-a-b4{0.0%{opacity:0.25}53.6%{opacity:0.25}56.6%{opacity:1}100.0%{opacity:1}}.tran-a-b4{animation:tran-a-b4 9s linear infinite}@keyframes tran-a-b5{0.0%{opacity:0.25}62.0%{opacity:0.25}65.0%{opacity:1}100.0%{opacity:1}}.tran-a-b5{animation:tran-a-b5 9s linear infinite}</style>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="18" y="28" class="tran-hd" font-size="16">ONE RAY, THREE CURVES &#8212; why T(t) does the occluding</text>
<text x="1142" y="28" text-anchor="end" fill="#f0883e" font-size="14">illustrative ray, not a measurement from the paper</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="The scene along one ray" data-tip="A ray leaves the camera, crosses empty air, grazes a thin translucent surface, then meets an opaque wall. Everything past the wall is still in the volume and the MLP still has an opinion about its colour, but no light from it reaches the camera.">
<rect x="18" y="44" width="1122" height="112" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="42" y="72" class="tran-t" font-size="16">The ray</text>
<g data-tiphead="What the ray passes through" data-tip="Empty air, then a thin translucent pane, then an opaque wall, and finally solid content that the wall completely hides.">
<path d="M120,116 L1108,116" stroke="#666666" stroke-width="2"/>
<path d="M104,106 L104,126 L124,116 z" fill="#3b82f6"/>
<rect x="470" y="88" width="18" height="56" rx="3" fill="#3fb950" opacity="0.35"/>
<rect x="676" y="76" width="34" height="80" rx="3" fill="#f0883e" opacity="0.55"/>
<rect x="828" y="88" width="200" height="56" rx="3" fill="#666666" opacity="0.28"/>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="Reading the three panels together" data-tip="Follow the ray from the camera: each sample adds its density bar, T(t) falls by what that sample absorbed, and the pixel weight is whatever T was still left times the opacity of that sample. Illustrative values, not a measurement."><circle class="tran-a-ball" cx="104" cy="116" r="8" fill="#f0f0f0" opacity="0"/></g>
<text x="104" y="96" class="tran-d" font-size="14">camera</text>
<text x="479" y="82" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3fb950" font-size="14">thin glass</text>
<text x="693" y="70" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0883e" font-size="14">opaque wall</text>
<text x="928" y="82" text-anchor="middle" class="tran-d" font-size="14">solid, but hidden behind the wall</text>
<circle cx="200" cy="116" r="5" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<circle cx="340" cy="116" r="5" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<circle cx="479" cy="116" r="5" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<circle cx="693" cy="116" r="5" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<circle cx="880" cy="116" r="5" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<circle cx="1000" cy="116" r="5" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<text x="200" y="142" text-anchor="middle" class="tran-d" font-size="14">1</text>
<text x="340" y="142" text-anchor="middle" class="tran-d" font-size="14">2</text>
<text x="479" y="142" text-anchor="middle" class="tran-d" font-size="14">3</text>
<text x="693" y="142" text-anchor="middle" class="tran-d" font-size="14">4</text>
<text x="880" y="142" text-anchor="middle" class="tran-d" font-size="14">5</text>
<text x="1000" y="142" text-anchor="middle" class="tran-d" font-size="14">6</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Density along the ray" data-tip="Sigma is what the MLP outputs at each sample. It is near zero in air, moderate in the glass and large in the wall. On its own it says nothing about visibility: the wall and the object hidden behind it both have high density.">
<rect x="18" y="172" width="366" height="188" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="42" y="200" fill="#f0883e" font-size="17" font-weight="700">&#963;(t): what the MLP says is there</text>
<g data-tiphead="Density bars" data-tip="One bar per sample. The two bars on the right are inside solid content that sits behind the wall, and their density is just as high as the wall itself.">
<path d="M46,330 L360,330" stroke="#3a3a3a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<path d="M46,216 L46,330" stroke="#3a3a3a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<rect opacity="0.25" class="tran-a-b0" x="66" y="327" width="18" height="3" fill="#f0883e"/>
<rect opacity="0.25" class="tran-a-b1" x="110" y="327" width="18" height="3" fill="#f0883e"/>
<rect opacity="0.25" class="tran-a-b2" x="154" y="306" width="18" height="24" fill="#f0883e"/>
<rect opacity="0.25" class="tran-a-b3" x="222" y="240" width="18" height="90" fill="#f0883e"/>
<rect opacity="0.25" class="tran-a-b4" x="280" y="228" width="18" height="102" fill="#f0883e"/>
<rect opacity="0.25" class="tran-a-b5" x="324" y="228" width="18" height="102" fill="#f0883e"/>
</g>
<text x="52" y="346" class="tran-d" font-size="14">air</text>
<text x="163" y="346" text-anchor="middle" class="tran-d" font-size="14">glass</text>
<text x="231" y="346" text-anchor="middle" class="tran-d" font-size="14">wall</text>
<text x="333" y="346" text-anchor="middle" class="tran-d" font-size="14">behind</text>
<text x="60" y="236" class="tran-d" font-size="14">high &#963; behind the wall too</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Transmittance along the ray" data-tip="T is the running product of what got through so far. It leaves the camera at 1, dips slightly in the glass and collapses at the wall. Past the wall it is essentially zero, so whatever the MLP claims is back there is multiplied away.">
<rect x="396" y="172" width="366" height="188" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="418" y="200" fill="#3fb950" font-size="17" font-weight="700">T(t): how much light arrives</text>
<g data-tiphead="The transmittance curve" data-tip="Monotone by construction: the exponent only accumulates, so T can never recover once it has fallen.">
<path d="M424,330 L738,330" stroke="#3a3a3a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<path d="M424,216 L424,330" stroke="#3a3a3a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<path opacity="0.25" d="M424,224 L544,224 L544,246 L600,246 L600,318 L660,318 L660,329 L738,329" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2.6" fill="none"/>
<path class="tran-a-T" d="M424,224 L544,224 L544,246 L600,246 L600,318 L660,318 L660,329 L738,329" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2.6" fill="none"/>
</g>
<text x="432" y="244" fill="#3fb950" font-size="14">T = 1.00</text>
<text x="732" y="314" text-anchor="end" fill="#3fb950" font-size="14">T = 0.00</text>
<text x="418" y="346" class="tran-d" font-size="14">Monotone: it can only fall, never recover.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4.E3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="The weight the pixel actually uses" data-tip="The product of transmittance and opacity is the weight each sample gets in the final colour. Most of it lands on the first opaque surface, with a smaller share on the glass in front of it, which is exactly the behaviour you want and the same quantity the hierarchical sampler reuses as a distribution.">
<rect x="774" y="172" width="366" height="188" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#93c5fd" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="796" y="200" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="17" font-weight="700">w = T &#183; &#945;: the pixel weights</text>
<g data-tiphead="The weight bars" data-tip="Most of the mass lands on the wall, the first opaque surface; the glass takes a smaller share. The two samples behind the wall are multiplied by a transmittance of nearly zero and vanish.">
<path d="M802,330 L1116,330" stroke="#3a3a3a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<path d="M802,216 L802,330" stroke="#3a3a3a" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<rect opacity="0.25" class="tran-a-b0" x="822" y="327" width="18" height="3" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<rect opacity="0.25" class="tran-a-b1" x="866" y="327" width="18" height="3" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<rect opacity="0.25" class="tran-a-b2" x="910" y="308" width="18" height="22" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<rect opacity="0.25" class="tran-a-b3" x="978" y="252" width="18" height="78" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<rect opacity="0.25" class="tran-a-b4" x="1036" y="321" width="18" height="9" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<rect opacity="0.25" class="tran-a-b5" x="1080" y="329" width="18" height="1" fill="#93c5fd"/>
</g>
<text x="796" y="346" class="tran-d" font-size="14">Most weight on the wall; here weights sum to 1.</text>
<text x="812" y="240" class="tran-d" font-size="14">the visible surface</text>
</a>
<rect x="18" y="376" width="551" height="96" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="42" y="406" class="tran-t" font-size="17">Why &#963; alone is not enough</text>
<text x="42" y="434" class="tran-d" font-size="15">Sample 6 sits inside a solid object and has high density, so on</text>
<text x="42" y="454" class="tran-d" font-size="15">its own it would contribute colour. T(t) is what silences it.</text>
<rect x="589" y="376" width="551" height="96" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#93c5fd" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="613" y="406" class="tran-t" font-size="17">Where the two roles split</text>
<text x="613" y="434" class="tran-d" font-size="15">&#963; is local and looks only at this point. T is cumulative and</text>
<text x="613" y="454" class="tran-d" font-size="15">looks at everything between the camera and this point.</text>
<rect x="18" y="488" width="1122" height="94" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="42" y="516" class="tran-t" font-size="17">The consequence worth remembering</text>
<text x="42" y="542" class="tran-d" font-size="15">Occlusion is not a special case in NeRF, and there is no visibility test anywhere in the code. It is one multiplication:</text>
<text x="42" y="566" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15" font-weight="700">once T has collapsed, everything further along the ray is multiplied by nearly zero and stops mattering.</text>
</svg>
</div>

<a class="slide-id" id="a306d5b9-ff3b-4162-a6eb-15894ca4889a"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm rawhead tight -->

## Six samples, worked through, so the symbols stop being symbols

| sample | where it is | σᵢδᵢ | αᵢ = 1 − e<sup>−σᵢδᵢ</sup> | Tᵢ | wᵢ = Tᵢαᵢ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | air | 0.01 | 0.01 | 1.00 | 0.01 |
| 2 | air | 0.01 | 0.01 | 0.99 | 0.01 |
| 3 | thin glass | 0.22 | 0.20 | 0.98 | 0.20 |
| 4 | **the wall** | 2.30 | **0.90** | **0.78** | **0.70** |
| 5 | behind the wall | 3.00 | 0.95 | 0.08 | 0.08 |
| 6 | behind the wall | 3.00 | 0.95 | 0.00 | 0.00 |

- **Illustrative densities, invented for this walk-through** — no such table appears in the paper
- Sample 6 is *solid*: high density, and still contributes nothing, because **Tᵢ has already collapsed**; σ itself is **never negative** — a ReLU rectifies it *(Fig. 7)*
- Here the weights sum to **1.00** because the wall stops the ray, so Ĉ(r) is a weighted average. A ray that **hits nothing** keeps leftover transmittance and its weights sum to **less than 1**: the rest is transmitted past the far bound
- **What fills that gap is not in the paper**; the released code composites the synthetic scenes onto **a white background** and treats the last sample's δ as effectively infinite
- On the **real forward-facing scenes** the volume reaches to infinity: depth is mapped into [−1, 1] in normalized device coordinates *(supplement A)*, so distant background is inside the volume, not left over

<a class="slide-id" id="b417e6ca-004c-4273-b7fc-2690ab5a99ab"></a>

<!-- _class: fig-720 -->

## The integral compiles down to alpha compositing

<p style="text-align:center; margin:0 0 2px"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="500" style="background:#fff; border-radius:6px; padding:3px 10px"/></p>
<p class="ev" style="text-align:center; margin:0">Equation 3 as printed in <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08934">Mildenhall et al. 2020</a>, p. 6 — the figure takes it apart.</p>
<p style="text-align:center; margin:4px 0 0; font-size:19px"><b>From Eq. 1 to Eq. 3:</b> hold σ constant on each slab, so T(tᵢ) = exp(−Σ<sub>j&lt;i</sub> σⱼδⱼ) = Π<sub>j&lt;i</sub> e<sup>−σⱼδⱼ</sup> = Π<sub>j&lt;i</sub> (1 − αⱼ)</p>
<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.2rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="860" height="445" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">
<style>.quad-t{fill:#f0f0f0;font-weight:700}.quad-m{font-family:'JetBrains Mono',monospace}.quad-d{fill:#a0a0a0}.quad-hd{fill:#3b82f6;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.05em}</style>
<defs>
<marker id="qg" markerWidth="12" markerHeight="12" refX="9" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#3b82f6"/></marker>
</defs>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="18" y="28" class="quad-hd" font-size="16">FROM INTEGRAL TO CODE &#8212; stratified samples, then alpha compositing</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4.E3" target="_blank"><text x="1142" y="28" text-anchor="end" class="quad-d" font-size="14">Sec. 4, Eq. 2 and Eq. 3</text></a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4.E2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Equation 2: stratified sampling" data-tip="The span between the near and far bounds is cut into N equal bins and one sample is drawn uniformly at random inside each bin. A fixed grid would pin the representation to a fixed resolution; randomising inside the bins means that across training steps the MLP is asked about every position in the interval, so the learned field stays continuous.">
<rect x="18" y="44" width="1122" height="150" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="42" y="74" class="quad-t" font-size="17">Step 1 &#8212; cut the ray into N bins, then jitter one sample inside each</text>
<g data-tiphead="One draw per bin" data-tip="The bin edges are fixed; the sample inside each bin is not. Over many steps every position in the interval gets queried.">
<path d="M60,142 L1112,142" stroke="#666666" stroke-width="2"/>
<path d="M60,126 L60,158 M235,126 L235,158 M410,126 L410,158 M585,126 L585,158 M760,126 L760,158 M935,126 L935,158 M1110,126 L1110,158" stroke="#3a3a3a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<circle cx="128" cy="142" r="6" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<circle cx="368" cy="142" r="6" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<circle cx="452" cy="142" r="6" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<circle cx="672" cy="142" r="6" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<circle cx="800" cy="142" r="6" fill="#93c5fd"/>
<circle cx="1052" cy="142" r="6" fill="#93c5fd"/>
</g>
<text x="60" y="116" class="quad-d" font-size="14">near bound</text>
<text x="1112" y="116" text-anchor="end" class="quad-d" font-size="14">far bound</text>
<text x="42" y="180" class="quad-d" font-size="15">Random inside each bin, not a fixed grid, so the MLP is queried at continuous positions and the field it learns is continuous.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4.E3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Equation 3: the quadrature rule" data-tip="Between two adjacent samples the density is treated as constant over a slab of thickness delta. The chance that the ray is stopped inside that slab is one minus exp of minus sigma delta, which is exactly an alpha value, and the running product of the alphas that came before it is the discrete transmittance.">
<rect x="18" y="210" width="1122" height="176" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#bc8cff" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="42" y="240" class="quad-t" font-size="17">Step 2 &#8212; treat each gap as a slab of constant density</text>
<text x="42" y="284" class="quad-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="22">&#264;(r) = &#931;&#7522; T&#7522; &#945;&#7522; c&#7522;</text>
<g data-tiphead="Alpha, the opacity of one slab" data-tip="Density is a rate per unit length. Multiplying by the slab thickness and passing it through one minus exp gives the fraction of light the slab stops.">
<rect x="352" y="256" width="252" height="76" rx="8" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="372" y="284" class="quad-m" fill="#f0883e" font-size="17">&#945;&#7522; = 1 - exp(-&#963;&#7522; &#948;&#7522;)</text>
<text x="372" y="312" class="quad-d" font-size="14">how opaque this slab is</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="Discrete transmittance" data-tip="The running product of one minus alpha over every earlier slab: how much light was still travelling when the ray reached this sample.">
<rect x="622" y="256" width="252" height="76" rx="8" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="642" y="284" class="quad-m" fill="#3fb950" font-size="17">T&#7522; = &#928; (1 - &#945;&#11002;)</text>
<text x="642" y="312" class="quad-d" font-size="14">what survived the slabs before</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="Delta, the slab thickness" data-tip="The distance to the next sample along the ray. It is what converts a density into an opacity, and it is why a thin dense slab and a thick thin one can block the same light.">
<rect x="892" y="256" width="230" height="76" rx="8" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#bc8cff" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="912" y="284" class="quad-m" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="17">&#948;&#7522; = t&#7522;&#8330;&#8321; - t&#7522;</text>
<text x="912" y="312" class="quad-d" font-size="14">gap to the next sample</text>
</g>
<text x="42" y="356" class="quad-d" font-size="15">Density is a rate per unit length, so it only becomes an opacity once multiplied by a thickness. That is the job of &#948;&#7522;:</text>
<text x="42" y="376" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15" font-weight="700">a thin slab of dense fog and a thick slab of thin fog can block exactly the same amount of light.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4.E3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="It is alpha compositing" data-tip="Written this way the render is the front-to-back over operator that every graphics pipeline already implements. The paper says so explicitly: the function reduces to traditional alpha compositing with alpha values one minus exp of minus sigma delta.">
<rect x="18" y="402" width="551" height="180" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#93c5fd" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="42" y="432" class="quad-t" font-size="17">You have written this loop before</text>
<text x="42" y="464" class="quad-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15">C = 0; T = 1</text>
<text x="42" y="488" class="quad-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15">for each sample i, front to back:</text>
<text x="42" y="512" class="quad-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15">    C += T * &#945;&#7522; * c&#7522;</text>
<text x="42" y="536" class="quad-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15">    T *= (1 - &#945;&#7522;)</text>
<text x="42" y="564" class="quad-d" font-size="15">Front-to-back alpha compositing, exactly as in Eq. 3.</text>
</a>
<rect x="589" y="402" width="551" height="180" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="613" y="432" class="quad-t" font-size="17">Three consequences that matter</text>
<text x="613" y="466" class="quad-d" font-size="15">&#183; Differentiable: sums, products, exponentials. The paper</text>
<text x="629" y="486" class="quad-d" font-size="15">calls it trivially differentiable, so gradients reach &#920;.</text>
<text x="613" y="514" class="quad-d" font-size="15">&#183; The weights T&#7522;&#945;&#7522; are reused as a sampling PDF (Eq. 5).</text>
<text x="613" y="542" class="quad-d" font-size="15">&#183; Cost is linear in samples per ray, so rendering is slow:</text>
<text x="629" y="562" class="quad-d" font-size="15">256 network queries for every single pixel.</text>
</svg>
</div>

<a class="slide-id" id="c528f7db-1115-4384-08fd-379ab1ba0abc"></a>

## The only teacher is a photograph you already had

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.4rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="980" height="507" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">
<style>.grad-t{fill:#f0f0f0;font-weight:700}.grad-m{font-family:'JetBrains Mono',monospace}.grad-d{fill:#a0a0a0}.grad-hd{fill:#3b82f6;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.05em}</style>
<defs>
<marker id="gg" markerWidth="12" markerHeight="12" refX="9" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#3b82f6"/></marker>
<marker id="gr" markerWidth="12" markerHeight="12" refX="9" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#f85149"/></marker>
</defs>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="18" y="28" class="grad-hd" font-size="16">WHERE THE GRADIENT COMES FROM &#8212; there is no 3D supervision</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S5.E6" target="_blank"><text x="1142" y="28" text-anchor="end" class="grad-d" font-size="14">Sec. 5.3, Eq. 6</text></a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S5.SS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="The supervision signal" data-tip="Every training step picks 4096 rays at random from the pool of all pixels in all training photographs. Each ray is rendered twice, coarse and fine, and both renders are scored against the same single number: the colour that pixel already has in the photograph.">
<rect x="18" y="44" width="1122" height="204" rx="12" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="42" y="74" class="grad-t" font-size="17">One training step, drawn honestly</text>
<g data-tiphead="The data" data-tip="The training photographs, each with a known camera pose. Rays are drawn from the pool of all pixels in all training images, not one image at a time.">
<rect x="42" y="92" width="176" height="84" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="130" y="120" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-t" font-size="15">all training photos</text>
<text x="130" y="142" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-d" font-size="14">each with a known pose</text>
<text x="130" y="162" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-d" font-size="14">4096 random pixels</text>
</g>
<path d="M224,134 L258,134" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#gg)" fill="none"/>
<g data-tiphead="The forward pass" data-tip="Every chosen ray is marched, encoded, pushed through the MLP and composited, twice: once through the coarse network and once through the fine one.">
<rect x="268" y="92" width="176" height="84" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="356" y="120" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-t" font-size="15">render those rays</text>
<text x="356" y="142" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-d" font-size="14">MLP then quadrature</text>
<text x="356" y="162" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-d" font-size="14">coarse and fine</text>
</g>
<path d="M450,134 L484,134" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#gg)" fill="none"/>
<g data-tiphead="The comparison" data-tip="Total squared error between rendered and true pixel colours, for both the coarse and the fine render. That is Equation 6 in full.">
<rect x="494" y="92" width="220" height="84" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="604" y="118" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-t" font-size="15">compare, per pixel</text>
<text x="604" y="144" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-m" fill="#f85149" font-size="15">&#8214;&#264;&#7580;-C&#8214;&#178; + &#8214;&#264;&#7584;-C&#8214;&#178;</text>
<text x="604" y="165" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-d" font-size="14">total squared error</text>
</g>
<path d="M720,134 L754,134" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#gg)" fill="none"/>
<g data-tiphead="The objective" data-tip="One scalar, measured entirely in image space. Nothing in it refers to a surface, a depth or an occupancy.">
<rect x="764" y="92" width="176" height="84" rx="8" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#93c5fd" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="852" y="128" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-t" font-size="15">one scalar loss</text>
<text x="852" y="152" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-d" font-size="14">measured in pixels</text>
</g>
<path d="M946,134 L980,134" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#gg)" fill="none"/>
<g data-tiphead="The update" data-tip="Adam, with a learning rate that decays exponentially over the run, applied to the weights of both networks.">
<rect x="990" y="92" width="126" height="84" rx="8" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="1053" y="128" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-t" font-size="15">Adam step</text>
<text x="1053" y="152" text-anchor="middle" class="grad-d" font-size="14">on &#920;</text>
</g>
<path d="M1053,184 L1053,212 L356,212 L356,186" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="2.6" stroke-dasharray="9 6" marker-end="url(#gr)" fill="none"/>
<text x="705" y="234" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f85149" font-size="16" font-weight="700">&#8706;L / &#8706;&#920; back through the quadrature</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Why the chain rule survives the renderer" data-tip="The sample positions are constants once drawn, and everything after them is a sum of products of smooth functions. So the derivative of the pixel error with respect to every density and colour the MLP produced exists, and from there ordinary backpropagation carries it into the weights.">
<rect x="18" y="264" width="551" height="168" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="42" y="294" class="grad-t" font-size="17">Why the error can reach the weights</text>
<text x="42" y="324" class="grad-d" font-size="15">Sample positions are constants for the step. Everything after</text>
<text x="42" y="346" class="grad-d" font-size="15">them is sums, products and exponentials of the MLP outputs.</text>
<text x="42" y="374" class="grad-d" font-size="15">So the derivative of the loss with respect to each &#963; and each</text>
<text x="42" y="396" class="grad-d" font-size="15">c exists in closed form, and backpropagation does the rest.</text>
<text x="42" y="422" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15" font-weight="700">Geometry is learned as a by-product of matching pixels.</text>
</a>
<rect x="589" y="264" width="551" height="168" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="613" y="294" fill="#f85149" font-size="17" font-weight="700">What is never in the loss</text>
<text x="613" y="324" class="grad-d" font-size="15">&#215;&#160; depth maps or laser scans</text>
<text x="613" y="350" class="grad-d" font-size="15">&#215;&#160; meshes, point clouds, voxel occupancy targets</text>
<text x="613" y="376" class="grad-d" font-size="15">&#215;&#160; silhouettes, masks or background plates</text>
<text x="613" y="400" class="grad-d" font-size="15">&#215;&#160; any regulariser on the shape of the density field</text>
<text x="613" y="422" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15" font-weight="700">The abstract says it: the only input is posed images.</text>
<rect x="18" y="448" width="1122" height="134" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="42" y="478" class="grad-t" font-size="17">The consequence readers underrate</text>
<text x="42" y="506" class="grad-d" font-size="15">Nothing tells the network where surfaces are. What pushes it to a coherent 3D shape is that one density field has to explain</text>
<text x="42" y="528" class="grad-d" font-size="15">every training photograph at once. That is an argument, not a proof: the paper shows only that quality falls as views are cut.</text>
<text x="42" y="558" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15" font-weight="700">Table 2: 31.01 PSNR with 100 views, 29.79 with 50, 27.78 with 25. Multi-view consistency is not a loss term here.</text>
</svg>
</div>

<a class="slide-id" id="d639a8ec-2226-4495-190e-48a2c2cb1bbd"></a>

## Raw coordinates give a blur; a fixed change of basis fixes it

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.4rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="980" height="507" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">
<style>.pose-t{fill:#f0f0f0;font-weight:700}.pose-m{font-family:'JetBrains Mono',monospace}.pose-d{fill:#a0a0a0}.pose-hd{fill:#3b82f6;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.05em}</style>
<defs>
<marker id="eg" markerWidth="12" markerHeight="12" refX="9" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#3b82f6"/></marker>
</defs>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="18" y="28" class="pose-hd" font-size="16">POSITIONAL ENCODING &#8212; the MLP was never the bottleneck</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S5.SS1" target="_blank"><text x="1142" y="28" text-anchor="end" class="pose-d" font-size="14">Sec. 5.1, Eq. 4</text></a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S5.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="The failure that motivates it" data-tip="Feeding raw coordinates in, the network must express a rapidly varying function of a slowly varying input. Rahaman et al. showed deep networks are biased towards learning lower frequency functions, so what comes out is a smooth blur: correct at low frequency, missing every edge and texture.">
<rect x="18" y="44" width="551" height="200" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="42" y="74" fill="#f85149" font-size="17" font-weight="700">Feed raw (x, y, z) and you get a blur</text>
<g data-tiphead="Raw coordinates" data-tip="A position normalised to the range minus 1 to 1, plus the viewing direction. Two points a hair apart look almost identical to the first layer.">
<rect x="42" y="90" width="114" height="48" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="99" y="120" text-anchor="middle" class="pose-t" font-size="15">(x,y,z,&#952;,&#966;)</text>
</g>
<path d="M162,114 L186,114" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#eg)" fill="none"/>
<g data-tiphead="The same MLP" data-tip="Nothing is wrong with the network. It is a universal approximator; it is simply biased toward the low-frequency end.">
<rect x="196" y="90" width="100" height="48" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="246" y="120" text-anchor="middle" class="pose-t" font-size="15">MLP</text>
</g>
<path d="M302,114 L326,114" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#eg)" fill="none"/>
<g data-tiphead="The result" data-tip="Right in the large and wrong at every edge. Figure 4 shows geometry and texture washing out into a soft blob.">
<rect x="340" y="90" width="206" height="48" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="443" y="120" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f85149" font-size="15" font-weight="700">oversmoothed render</text>
</g>
<text x="42" y="168" class="pose-d" font-size="15">Positions are first scaled to [&#8722;1, 1]. Deep networks are biased</text>
<text x="42" y="190" class="pose-d" font-size="15">towards lower frequency functions, so the fit is right in the</text>
<text x="42" y="212" class="pose-d" font-size="15">large and wrong at every edge. Table 2 row 2: 28.77 PSNR</text>
<text x="42" y="232" class="pose-d" font-size="15">against 31.01, and Fig. 4 shows what that looks like.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S5.E4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Equation 4: the encoding itself" data-tip="Gamma maps one scalar to a ladder of sines and cosines at frequencies that double: 2 to the 0, 2 to the 1, up to 2 to the L minus 1, each times pi times the coordinate. It has no parameters and learns nothing. Nearby coordinates that a network would otherwise struggle to separate get very different high-frequency components, so the MLP can turn a sharp corner over a tiny change in position.">
<rect x="589" y="44" width="551" height="200" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="613" y="74" fill="#f0883e" font-size="17" font-weight="700">Lift the coordinate first, then learn</text>
<text x="613" y="112" class="pose-m" fill="#f0883e" font-size="17">&#947;(p) = ( sin(2&#8304;&#960;p), cos(2&#8304;&#960;p), &#8230; ,</text>
<text x="661" y="138" class="pose-m" fill="#f0883e" font-size="17">sin(2&#7488;&#8315;&#185;&#960;p), cos(2&#7488;&#8315;&#185;&#960;p) )</text>
<path d="M613,180 q14,-24 28,0 q14,24 28,0 q14,-24 28,0 q14,24 28,0" stroke="#a0a0a0" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/>
<path d="M741,180 q7,-24 14,0 q7,24 14,0 q7,-24 14,0 q7,24 14,0 q7,-24 14,0 q7,24 14,0" stroke="#93c5fd" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/>
<path d="M869,180 q3.5,-24 7,0 q3.5,24 7,0 q3.5,-24 7,0 q3.5,24 7,0 q3.5,-24 7,0 q3.5,24 7,0 q3.5,-24 7,0 q3.5,24 7,0 q3.5,-24 7,0 q3.5,24 7,0" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/>
<text x="613" y="212" class="pose-d" font-size="15">No parameters, nothing learned: a fixed change of variables.</text>
<text x="613" y="232" class="pose-d" font-size="15">Two nearby points become far apart in the encoded space.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S5.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Why L differs for position and direction" data-tip="Position must carry texture and sharp geometric edges, so it gets ten octaves. Viewing direction only has to describe how appearance drifts as you walk around an object, which is a smooth function of angle, so four octaves are enough. Each scalar becomes 2L numbers, applied to all three components.">
<rect x="18" y="260" width="551" height="152" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="42" y="290" class="pose-t" font-size="17">Two different budgets, for a reason</text>
<g data-tiphead="Position budget" data-tip="Ten octaves per coordinate, so each of x, y and z becomes twenty numbers: sixty in total.">
<rect x="42" y="306" width="240" height="48" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="162" y="336" text-anchor="middle" class="pose-t" font-size="15">&#947;(x): L = 10, 3 &#8594; 60</text>
</g>
<g data-tiphead="Direction budget" data-tip="Four octaves per component, so the unit direction vector becomes twenty-four numbers.">
<rect x="302" y="306" width="240" height="48" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#bc8cff" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="422" y="336" text-anchor="middle" class="pose-t" font-size="15">&#947;(d): L = 4, 3 &#8594; 24</text>
</g>
<text x="42" y="380" class="pose-d" font-size="15">Position carries texture and hard edges. Direction only has</text>
<text x="42" y="400" class="pose-d" font-size="15">to describe smooth drift, so it needs far fewer octaves.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S6.T2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Where L stops paying" data-tip="Rows 7 and 8 of Table 2 sweep the number of frequencies for position. Five is too few and costs quality; fifteen buys nothing over ten. The paper attributes the ceiling to two to the L exceeding the maximum frequency present in the input images, roughly 1024 in their data. Positions are normalised to the range minus 1 to 1 before encoding, so the frequencies are relative to the scene volume; the paper gives no units for the 1024.">
<rect x="589" y="260" width="551" height="152" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="613" y="290" class="pose-t" font-size="17">More frequencies stop helping, and why</text>
<text x="613" y="320" class="pose-d" font-size="15">Table 2, rows 7 to 9, on the realistic synthetic scenes:</text>
<text x="613" y="352" class="pose-m" fill="#a0a0a0" font-size="16">L = 5: 30.59&#160;&#160;&#160;L = 10: 31.01&#160;&#160;&#160;L = 15: 30.81</text>
<text x="613" y="380" class="pose-d" font-size="14">Paper: the gain stops once 2 to the L passes the highest frequency</text>
<text x="613" y="400" class="pose-d" font-size="14">in the images, roughly 1024 = 2 to the 10: L = 10 is the ceiling.</text>
</a>
<rect x="18" y="428" width="1122" height="154" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="42" y="456" class="pose-t" font-size="17">The idea underneath, worth stealing on its own</text>
<text x="42" y="484" class="pose-d" font-size="15">The network was never the bottleneck. A coordinate MLP fed raw coordinates must represent a high-frequency function of a</text>
<text x="42" y="506" class="pose-d" font-size="15">low-frequency input &#8212; exactly the regime it is biased against. Changing the input basis moves the problem into a regime</text>
<text x="42" y="528" class="pose-d" font-size="15">the same network handles easily: no extra depth, no extra width, no extra parameters.</text>
<text x="42" y="554" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15" font-weight="700">Same trigonometric family as the Transformer positional encoding, used for an unrelated purpose. There it injects</text>
<text x="42" y="574" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="15" font-weight="700">discrete order into an order-blind architecture; here it lifts continuous coordinates so an MLP can fit sharp detail.</text>
</svg>
</div>

---

<marker id="hg" markerWidth="12" markerHeight="12" refX="9" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#3b82f6"/></marker>

<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="18" y="28" class="hier-hd" font-size="16">HIERARCHICAL SAMPLING &#8212; the coarse net says where the fine one looks</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S5.SS2" target="_blank"><text x="1142" y="28" text-anchor="end" class="hier-d" font-size="14">Sec. 5.2, Eq. 5</text></a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S5.SS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Step 1: the coarse network" data-tip="Sixty-four samples are spread over the whole ray by stratified sampling and pushed through the coarse network. Most of them land in empty space or behind the first surface, where they contribute almost nothing to the pixel, so this pass is deliberately cheap and deliberately wasteful.">
<rect x="18" y="44" width="1122" height="128" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="42" y="74" fill="#3fb950" font-size="17" font-weight="700">1 &#183; Coarse network: 64 stratified samples, spread evenly and mostly wasted</text>
<g data-tiphead="Evenly spread samples" data-tip="Sixty-four positions covering the entire near-to-far interval. Most of them are in air or behind the surface and contribute nothing.">
<path d="M60,122 L1112,122" stroke="#666666" stroke-width="2"/>
<rect x="612" y="104" width="40" height="36" rx="3" fill="#f0883e" opacity="0.5"/>

<path d="M700,248 L740,248" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#hg)" fill="none"/>

</g>

<a class="slide-id" id="d89215c2-db96-49d0-9020-95400133193c"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## Two networks, 64 + 192 = 256 queries per ray, and a loss term for each

| network | evaluated at | produces | in the loss (Eq. 6) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **coarse** | 64 stratified samples | Ĉc(r), and the weights wᵢ | ‖Ĉc(r) − C(r)‖² |
| **fine** | the same 64 **plus** 128 drawn from wᵢ: **192** | Ĉf(r), the image you see | ‖Ĉf(r) − C(r)‖² |
| **total** | **256 network queries per ray** at render time *(supplement A)* | | |

- **The 64 coarse positions are queried twice**, once by each network — two sets of weights, so two different answers.
- **Inverse transform sampling, in three steps:** (1) the running sum of the normalised weights ŵᵢ is a CDF along the ray, rising from 0 to 1; (2) draw 128 uniform numbers in [0, 1]; (3) put each sample where the CDF crosses its number. **Where wᵢ is large the CDF is steep**, so most of the 128 land there. The released code then sorts all 192 by depth and recomputes each δᵢ before Eq. 3; the paper says only "the union".
- **Why the coarse render is scored too:** the image comes from Ĉf alone, but the paper also minimises the coarse loss **"so that the weight distribution from the coarse network can be used to allocate samples in the fine network"**. The fine pass uses the coarse network only to place samples, so this term is what teaches the coarse network where surfaces are.

## Geometry emerges even though nothing supervised it

<figure class="credit"><video class="clip" src="https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~viscomp/projects/LF/papers/ECCV20/nerf/website_renders/depth_ornament.mp4" style="width:860px;height:329px" data-autoplay muted loop playsinline controls preload="metadata"><a href="https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~viscomp/projects/LF/papers/ECCV20/nerf/website_renders/depth_ornament.mp4" target="_blank" rel="noopener">depth_ornament.mp4 on the NeRF project site</a></video><figcaption>Clip from the <a class="project" href="https://www.matthewtancik.com/nerf">project page</a>, section Geometry Visualization — not a PDF figure.</figcaption></figure>

| what you are seeing | why it is not free |
|---|---|
| depth = **expected ray termination**, Σᵢ wᵢtᵢ: the weight-averaged sample distance | **no depth was ever a target** — only pixel colours were |

- **Qualitative only:** the paper reports **no depth or geometry metric**; Σᵢ wᵢtᵢ is the read-out the released code uses, not an equation in the paper.

<a class="slide-id" id="1a7dccf0-666a-4d52-5e42-7b5f4fff5ff1"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-xs -->

## Best on eight of the nine numbers in Table 1 — and the ninth matters <span class="finfo" data-tiphead="Table forensics" data-tip="Every number is an average over the scenes in that dataset. There are no seeds, no confidence intervals, and no per-scene spread in the main body. Baselines were re-run by the authors on their data rather than copied, and the paper does not report equalised training budgets. NV has no entry on real forward-facing data because it only reconstructs objects inside a bounded volume.">ⓘ forensics</span>

| method | <span class="term" data-tiphead="Diffuse Synthetic 360°" data-tip="The DeepVoxels dataset: four Lambertian objects with simple geometry, rendered at 512 by 512 from the upper hemisphere, 479 views in and 1000 for testing.">Diffuse Synthetic 360°</span> | <span class="term" data-tiphead="Realistic Synthetic 360°" data-tip="The authors own dataset: eight pathtraced objects with complicated geometry and non-Lambertian materials, 100 views in and 200 for testing, all at 800 by 800.">Realistic Synthetic 360°</span> | <span class="term" data-tiphead="Real Forward-Facing" data-tip="Eight scenes captured with a handheld cellphone, five from the LLFF paper and three new, with 20 to 62 images each and one eighth held out for testing, at 1008 by 756.">Real Forward-Facing</span> |
|---|---|---|---|
| | PSNR↑ / SSIM↑ / LPIPS↓ | PSNR↑ / SSIM↑ / LPIPS↓ | PSNR↑ / SSIM↑ / LPIPS↓ |
| [SRN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01618) | 33.20 / 0.963 / 0.073 | 22.26 / 0.846 / 0.170 | 22.84 / 0.668 / 0.378 |
| [NV](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.07751) | 29.62 / 0.929 / 0.099 | 26.05 / 0.893 / 0.160 | not applicable |
| [LLFF](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.00889) | 34.38 / 0.985 / 0.048 | 24.88 / 0.911 / 0.114 | 24.13 / 0.798 / **0.212** |
| **NeRF** | **40.15 / 0.991 / 0.023** | **31.01 / 0.947 / 0.081** | **26.50 / 0.811** / 0.250 |

- **Metrics:** **PSNR** is pixel error in dB, higher is better, and +3 dB is about half the squared error; **SSIM** runs 0 to 1, higher is better, and compares local structure; **LPIPS** is a distance between deep features, lower is better, and tracks human judgement more closely
- Scope: four diffuse objects, eight pathtraced objects, eight handheld real captures — **no seeds, no error bars**; every method gets the same input views. NV and SRN run from **their authors' code and single-scene training procedure**, LLFF as **the authors' pretrained model** *(supplement B)*; no tuning is reported. **Compute is not matched**: NeRF fits for 1–2 days, the other per-scene methods at least 12 hours, LLFF under 10 minutes
- **LLFF wins <span class="term" data-tiphead="LPIPS" data-tip="Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity: the distance between deep features of the two images rather than their pixels, calibrated against human judgements. Lower is better, and it often disagrees with PSNR about which artefact is worse.">LPIPS</span> on the real scenes**, 0.212 against 0.250 — the paper answers with a video, not a number. **Verdict: a real loss**, on the perceptual metric and on the capture style LLFF was designed for; the multiview-consistency counterclaim stays unmeasured

<!-- _class: fs-xs -->

## Remove any one ingredient and PSNR drops <span class="finfo" data-tiphead="Table forensics" data-tip="All rows are averaged over the eight realistic synthetic scenes, with no seeds and no error bars. Rows 5 and 6 change the input data rather than the model, so they are not ablations of an architectural choice. The claim that 25 views still beats every baseline at 100 views is deferred to the supplementary material, which is not in the main body.">ⓘ forensics</span>

| row | what changes | PSNR↑ | SSIM↑ | LPIPS↓ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **all three removed**: raw xyz only, 256 coarse samples, one network | 26.67 | 0.906 | 0.136 |
| 2 | full model **minus positional encoding**: raw xyz and direction in | 28.77 | 0.924 | 0.108 |
| 3 | full model **minus view dependence**: xyz in, no direction | 27.66 | 0.925 | 0.117 |
| 4 | full model **minus hierarchical sampling**: one network, 256 coarse samples | 30.06 | 0.938 | 0.109 |
| 5 / 6 | **25 / 50** images, not 100 | 27.78 / 29.79 | 0.925 / 0.940 | 0.107 / 0.096 |
| 7 / 8 | **L = 5 / 15**, not 10 | 30.59 / 30.81 | 0.944 / 0.946 | 0.088 / 0.096 |
| **9** | **complete model** | **31.01** | **0.947** | **0.081** |

- Paper: **"positional encoding (row 2) and view-dependence (row 3) provide the largest quantitative benefit"** — PSNR puts **view dependence** first, 27.66 against 31.01, then the encoding, then the hierarchy; single runs, no error bars
- **Row 1 already beats NV** on the same eight scenes, 26.67 against 26.05 PSNR, and on SSIM and LPIPS too *(Table 1)*; **row 4 keeps the query budget**: 256 per ray in one network, against 64 + 192 in two
- **Fig. 4 suggests the opposite order** because it shows Lego, where dropping the encoding is worse (27.75 against 29.93); on shiny Materials it flips (24.96 against 27.79) *(supp. Table 6)*
- **The metrics disagree**: on LPIPS, dropping the encoding (0.108) ties dropping the hierarchy (0.109)

## What it cannot do, separated into concessions and silences

| limitation | evidence | conceded? |
|---|---|---|
| **static scenes only** | "We represent a static scene" — Sec 1 | by construction |
| **no cross-scene reuse** | one fit per scene | stated, never costed |
| **slow to render** | 30 s a frame, supplement | Sec 7, as future work |
| **accurate poses required** | COLMAP on real captures | stated as an input (Sec. 5.3); sensitivity never measured |
| **interpolation, not extrapolation** | test views come from the same capture: the same hemisphere or sphere of cameras for synthetic scenes, a held-out eighth of the same handheld sweep for real ones (Sec. 6.1) | never tested beyond |
| **no relighting or editing** | colour is *emitted*, lighting baked in; a gap of this method, which later work fills | silent |

- Sec 7 concedes two things: efficiency, and that **"it is unclear how to analyze these issues when we encode scenes in the weights of a deep neural network"**

<a class="slide-id" id="5eb10034-aa03-4196-9286-bf83333339f5"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## Challenge the assumptions

| claim | what is shown | what would settle it |
|---|---|---|
| encoding is decisive | Table 2 ranks it second by PSNR | seeds and error bars |
| it beats LLFF | eight of nine numbers | a perceptual test, not a video |
| 25 views suffice | cited to the supplement | the table itself |
| poses are just an input | never perturbed | a pose-noise sweep |
| renders are photorealistic | author-picked crops | crops chosen by a stated rule over all test views |

- **Mechanism proven, margins unmeasured** — no seeds or error bars anywhere
- Not contested: **5 MB against 15 GB** is too large a gap to be an artefact

<a class="slide-id" id="6fc21145-bb14-42a7-a397-c09444440af6"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## Steal list — checked against what already exists

| worth stealing | where | rough effort, presenter's estimate |
|---|---|---|
| lift coordinates before an MLP sees them | [Sec. 5.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S5.SS1) | a parameter-free layer — hours |
| supervise a differentiable renderer in image space | [Sec. 4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S4) | the renderer, not labels — weeks |
| enforce consistency by *withholding* an input | [Sec. 3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S3) | free, and the strongest idea here |
| reuse forward-pass weights as a sampling PDF | [Sec. 5.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S5.SS2) | one extra network, no new labels |
| store a signal as weights, not as a grid | [Sec. 6.3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2003.08934#S6.SS3) | days of fitting per instance |

- Where it went next: [relighting](https://pratulsrinivasan.github.io/nerv/) · [anti-aliasing](https://jonbarron.info/mipnerf/) · [fast fitting](https://www.matthewtancik.com/learnit) · [the encoding itself](https://bmild.github.io/fourfeat/)

<a class="slide-id" id="a6ec3730-2c99-4be3-970b-d69aee447fad"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## What to keep from this paper

1. **With posed images and no 3D labels, make the renderer differentiable and supervise in pixels** — squared colour error is the whole objective ([slide 17](#17)).
2. **Lift coordinates with fixed sines and cosines before any coordinate MLP sees them** — raw xyz gives a blur ([slides 18](#18), [24](#24)).
3. **Get consistency by withholding an input**: density never sees the viewing direction, so every camera must agree on the shape ([slide 8](#8)).
4. **Let a cheap pass's own weights decide where the expensive pass samples, and train the cheap pass for that job** ([slides 19–20](#19)).
5. **Budget one fit per scene, about 30 s per frame, and accurate poses** ([slides 27–28](#27)); later background: Instant-NGP and 3D Gaussian Splatting are built to cut exactly these costs.

**Starting today** (later practice, not from the paper): use a maintained successor such as [nerfstudio](https://docs.nerf.studio/) or [Instant-NGP](https://github.com/NVlabs/instant-ngp) for speed, and read this paper for the formulation.

**If you do one thing:** work the six-sample table on [slide 15](#15) by hand — Eq. 3 is the transferable idea.

---

<a class="slide-id" id="5f6a7b8c-9d0e-4f1a-b2c3-d4e5f6a7b8c9"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-lg -->

## Discussion — open questions for the group

- **The asymmetry is imposed, not learned.** Would a *soft* version buy anything on real captures — or just re-open the door to per-camera geometry?
- **256 queries per pixel.** Every fast successor attacks that number, not the representation. Which ingredient survives a real-time budget?
- **The scene is the weights.** What does diffing or partially updating a scene mean with no addressable geometry?
- **Poses are assumed exact.** Nothing measures what COLMAP error costs — is that why casual phone captures often disappoint?
